title: Emergency multisig use requires both potential harm and a vulnerability window that Executive Vote timing cannot close
content:
A.1.10.4.1.1.1 restricts the SparkLend Security Access Multisig to urgent or emergency situations and defines them with a conjunctive two-part test: "1) they have the potential to harm the Sky Ecosystem or SparkLend users; and 2) the preparation time required for an Executive Vote would leave the ecosystem vulnerable to harm."

Both limbs are load-bearing, and the second is the interesting one. It does not ask how bad the situation feels — it asks whether the *ordinary* governance path would have arrived in time. Severity alone does not license the emergency route; a severe but slow-moving problem still belongs in an Executive Vote.

This makes urgency a property of the relationship between threat timing and process latency, which is auditable after the fact. A reviewer can ask a concrete question: could a Spell have been prepared and voted before the harm landed? If yes, the multisig was misused, regardless of how justified the intervention looked.

The section also lists what the multisig is *for* — preventing technical vulnerabilities, unwanted contract functionality such as failing price oracles, and usage deviating from intended behaviour — and makes the Core Council responsible for ensuring use is "generally aligned" as well as compliant with the letter of these requirements.
description: The SparkLend two-part test makes urgency structural, not subjective: if a vote could have been prepared in time, the emergency path was not authorized.
